utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Ms. Benjamin, could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Tecla Henry-Benjamin and Andres Vatter, the case manager. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we have the appearances for Defence counsel, who are all present.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon and Fahrudin Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This will be the last hearing this week. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present, Ms. Benjamin, Defence counsel, who are all present today, as I have already said. I'd like to greet the accused and everyone else in the courtroom, the registrar, the legal officer, the usher, the court reporter, the assistants, and the security officers. And I won't forget to mention the interpreters in their booths either. The hearing that we'll be holding today will have to do with the hearing of a witness. I think that Ms. Benjamin wanted to mention a problem with the registry, but the registrar has said that we have a memo about this issue. We still haven't received this memo, though. Mr. Bourgon, is it necessary to make submissions now, since we aren't aware of the registry's position at the moment? Should we wait for the memo? I'll give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good day, Your Honours. Mr. President, just before the beginning of the hearing, I received a copy of the memo from the registry, and I believe that the Trial Chamber will be receiving it. I thought that perhaps there wouldn't be any memo. I do have the memo, though, and I have drawn the conclusions from it, and if necessary I will address the Chamber. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Ms. Benjamin, yesterday we mentioned a number of documents that were problematic. You said that you would make efforts to ensure that we were provided with these documents. In addition, there were some documents that didn't have any exhibit numbers; they only had OTP numbers. The Trial Chamber has examined the issue again and we have realised that there were other numbers that you did not mention. Could you do everything that is necessary in order to inform us, immediately perhaps or after the break, about this issue. Perhaps you could speak to the Chamber's legal officer about this matter, because we have realised that there are some numbers -- 948, 950, 963; those are the numbers I can remember -- there are some numbers that you did not mention, and we need all the relevant information. If you aren't in a position to provide us with this information now, you could do so at a later stage. If you want to provide us with any information now, you may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's our intention to deal with it at -- after the break or after this witness. I have discussed the matter with the Defence, and I'm ready to inform the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Benjamin. I'll now ask the usher to call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. I'd first like to make sure that you are receiving the interpretation of what I am saying. If so, please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We know that you arrived at about 11.00 at the airport and you were brought to the Tribunal immediately in order to speak to the Prosecution and perhaps to the Defence as well, because you've been called here as a witness for the Prosecution. Before you take the solemn declaration, I would like you to tell me your first and last names, your date of birth, and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Vinko Zrno. I was born on the 14th of September, 1954 in the village of Suica in Tomislavgrad Municipality in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I lived there Bugojno from 1978 until 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Are you currently employed? And if so, what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a construction technician. I work in Zagreb in Croatia, and I'm in charge of a construction site. I have full-time employment there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In 1993, over ten years ago, what sort of professional activities did you exercise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was again in charge of a construction site. I worked in the Gorica company in Bugojno, and I was a construction technician, as I am now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified before an international tribunal with regard to the events that took place in your country in 1993 or perhaps in a local court, or is this the first time that you will be testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never testified before in front of a national or international court. I have only given statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now ask you to read out the solemn declaration. The usher will show it to you. Please read it out in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said a minute ago, you have been called here as a witness for the Prosecution. The Prosecution are to your right, and in a minute they will start their examination-in-chief. After they have concluded their examination-in-chief -- and yesterday we were told that it might take one hour, perhaps less; we'll see -- after that stage, Defence counsel, who are to your left, will also ask you a series of questions. They will conduct what we call their cross-examination. The purpose of their questions will be to check the credibility of your statements and also to obtain information about the overall context within which these events referred to in the indictment occurred. Once Defence counsel has completed their cross-examination, the Prosecution may ask you additional questions. The three Judges sitting before you may also ask you questions in order to clarify some of your answers if they think this is necessary, or they may ask you questions if they believe that there are certain issues that should be raised because your testimony did not clarify certain issues that the Judges are interested in. In addition, as this procedure is mainly an oral procedure, your answers are important, so when answering questions, try to do so in a simple and precise terms so that the Judges can be well informed by what you say about what you saw and heard at the time. If you think that a question is very complicated, if you fail to understand the sense of a question, ask the person putting the question to you to rephrase it. There are two other elements I would like to point out: Firstly, you have taken the solemn declaration, which means that you should not give false testimony. You have sworn to speak the truth, so you are not supposed to lie when answering questions. In the case of false testimony, it's my duty to inform you that that constitutes a violation that can be punished by the Tribunal, either by a prison sentence or a fine. In addition - but this should not apply to you - if a question is put to the witness and the witness thinks that his answer could incriminate him, the witness may refuse to answer the question. In such a case, the Trial Chamber can compel the witness to answer the question, but the witness is guaranteed a form of immunity. But generally speaking, this should not be applicable to you. I've provided you with a rough sketch of the procedure that will be followed here. If you encounter difficulties of any kind, don't hesitate to inform us of the fact. We will rule and try to find a solution to the problem. Without wasting any more time, I will now let Ms. Benjamin take the floor. She will now commence the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Zrno, once again. Could you state for the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: -- you did compulsory national service with the JNA and for what period, please?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes. I did compulsory national service with the JNA from July 1976 until November 1977.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Subsequently to your service with the JNA, somewhere around -- in 1993 did you -- were you a member of any other military body?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: In 1993, I was a member of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you tell the Trial Chamber where you were stationed.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I was a guard in the military hospital which was in Kalin Hotel in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Trial Chamber the relationship between the Croats and the Muslims in Bugojno prior to April of 1993.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: The relationships between the Croats and the Muslims in Bugojno was excellent. The military hospital was a common one. There weren't any problems, and there were even a certain number of Muslims who were members of the HVO. There were no problems of any kind. I, at least, didn't notice any such problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did there come a time then, in 1993, when things began to change in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes. Things began to change in April 1993. That's when it started. And this continued to change until July, when the conflict broke out. There was tension in the town. This is something you could feel in the air. Something was going on. Something was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Zrno, could you tell us precisely when did the conflict begin in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I don't think I know the exact date, but I think it was around the 20th of July or the 18th of July. I'm not sure. All I know is that it was on a Monday. It started early in the morning on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And you personally, on the commencement of the conflict, did you do anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: My job was to guard the military hospital. That's what I did. I had to receive the wounded, provide them with assistance, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: At the beginning of the conflict, did you remain in the hotel compound?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Trial Chamber what you heard in the compound, whilst you were in the compound.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: As far as the conflict is concerned, the conflict broke out on Monday. On Sunday, I went to mass with my friends. The town was very silent. There was no movement of troops, and I happened to go to the military hospital where a colleague of mine was on duty. This colleague told me that two people -- two individuals had been killed. I think it was Mico Vucak and Telenta. There was a clash with the Muslims. He said that something was going on and that I had to go back quickly and put on my uniform. I went home, put my uniform on, reported for duty. As I said, it was very quiet until Monday morning. On Monday morning, everything started. Hell broke loose. There was shelling, shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And if you had to describe the situation in one word, how best would you be able to describe it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Terrible. You didn't know who was shooting on all sides -- from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you assist the Trial Chamber. For approximately how long did this shooting last?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Four or five days. From Monday - that's when it started - and it continued up until Friday. We surrendered on Saturday. It was a little quieter on Saturday, but it didn't stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, whilst the fighting was going on, what part of the -- the hotel were you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I was in the basement, which is where the military hospital was located. It was evacuated when this fighting was going on. One doctor remained and a nurse and two guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: As far as you know, did there come a time when the hotel was used as a shelter as well?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: The basement, which is where the military hospital was located, was never used as a shelter, at least not while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: On the other floors of the hotel, would you be able to assist us, who would have been on the other floors of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: On the ground floor, there was the military police, and two or three days after the fighting began, civilians came from a place called Gaj not far from the hotel. That's after Gaj had fallen. The civilians then came and they stayed on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Would you say that the hotel itself was a particular target during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And was there shooting -- much shooting at the hotel at all times during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did there come a time when there was a lull or break in the shooting?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Sometimes, but that was very seldom.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Well, did the shooting finally stop?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: The shooting stopped on Friday evening or Saturday morning, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber what you did upon realising that there was some cease-fire of some sort.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Well, sometime in the afternoon a colleague and I felt that things had quietened down. There was no more shooting. I asked him to remain in the basement. I went up to the ground floor, thinking that the police were up there. I wanted to see what was happening. When I arrived at the reception, the Muslim troops surrounded me. They insulted me. They said, "Lay your arms down, you Ustasha." I laid my weapon down. Then they went down to the basement with me, asked me who else was in there. I told them who was there. There was a wounded man there, a dead man, my colleague, as I said; there was a nurse and her husband and the doctor and the two guards. They took us outside. They didn't beat us or maltreat us. They treated us correctly. And then they took me and my colleague Stipica Jelavic to the secondary school. And the others they said they would take them to the medical centre, but I don't know if they did this.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You said to the Trial Chamber they were soldiers. Could you tell us who these soldiers were. Were you able to recognise how they were dressed, which unit they came from?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Well, their clothing was -- or their uniforms were a bit different from the HVO uniforms. It was the Muslim army. They had uniforms on, green berets, some sort of green bands on them or armbands.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And when you were being led out by these soldiers, could you tell us if you -- or are you able to tell us if the civilians that you told us about on the first floor were still in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I don't know where they were, what happened, because when I went up to the ground floor, I didn't see any of our civilians or any of our troops. I didn't see anyone. Only the Muslim troops were there, and there were a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said to us that you were escorted out by the Muslims, and could you tell us -- "the Muslim soldiers," to use your words -- and could you tell us where you were taken to, please.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: They took us to the Mahmut Busatlija Secondary School, which is 100 or 200 metres from the hotel. They took us out to the yard, and that's where the janitor received us. We spoke to him, had coffee with him. We spoke about what was happening, about the fact that the town was on fire and about how terrible the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: How close was the school to the Hotel Kalin?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: As I said, between 100 and 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And at the school, were you taken to anywhere in particular?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: At about 9.00 in the evening, they took us down to the basement, to a cell that was about 3 by 5 or 3 by 6 metres. There were no windows in it. There was not enough air there. There was only one door and there were some sort of bars. I think there were about 50 of us there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, you've more or less described the physical conditions for us. Could you tell us what eating arrangements were in place for you in the basement.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Well, while we were in the basement, they would provide us with one meal a day. That was provided for those who could go up and out into the courtyard, because it was chaotic during that conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What of bathroom facilities? Were you able to use the bathroom while in the basement?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: No. There wasn't even enough air, let alone a proper toilet. We had a bucket. And I apologise for having to describe that. We had a bucket that we used to relieve ourselves in. I have to say that amongst us there was a family, a husband, a wife, and two daughters. I believe that their family name was Misina [phoen] and he worked in the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, can you assist us with the ethnic background of the detainees in the basement.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: The people who were detained in the basement were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you were only allowed a meal when you went outside. Did you go outside eventually from the basement?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes. Once after three days, when I could no longer bear the hunger, I went up and I had a piece of bread and some pasta.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So previous to your going out after three days, is it your evidence that you had nothing to eat for three days while you were down in the basement? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You had meals while you were in the basement prior to your leaving the basement?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I did not have anything to eat. I've told you. I had nothing to eat for three days.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, why didn't you want to go out to have something to eat?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I was afraid that I would be beaten, because people were beaten continuously and you could hear them screaming and crying all the time. And it was not just me who was afraid; there were others who were afraid to go out.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Were you beaten while you were at the basement?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Do you know of any other people who were beaten in particular?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us your observations, please.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I remember very well. The guy whose name was Mario Subasic, he was pushed down the stairs and fell on the floor, and at that moment I could see his eye falling out of the eye socket and he was bleeding all over his face.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, during your stay or upon the arrival of your -- upon the arrival at the basement, were you allowed to have a change of clothing?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you actually changed your clothes?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So could you tell us: When you entered the basement, what clothing were you wearing?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: An HVO uniform, a military uniform with the insignia of the military hospital, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And did you continue to wear these clothes up until the time that you eventually left the basement?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes. Until the very day when we were transferred to the sports hall of the grammar school, from the day I put the uniform on when they told me that I had to go home and put it on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: When you got to the sports hall of the grammar school, could you briefly but concisely state to the Trial Chamber what transpired.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: We were given a little bit more space there. They accommodated us in the sports hall. A colleague of mine was there. He was a native of Bugojno. He visited Croatian houses. They were looking for volunteers that would bring us food. So some people were even allowed to change their clothes. They were given food. I myself volunteered to do that because I believed that it would allow me to change clothes and to be given some food. Unfortunately, I was wrong and we were taken in a different direction; we were taken to Vrbanja.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And did you remain at Vrbanja?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: When we were taken to Vrbanja, there were ten of us. Five were singled out to dig bodies along the Vrbas River, and the rest of us, the five of us, were taken up to the hill and we were asked to dig five graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: For what period of time was this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: It felt like an eternity.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: But approximately how much, in terms of days?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: What do you mean days? I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Approximately how long did you stay out there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I believe that we were taken around noon and that we stayed there until 3.00, 4.00, or 5.00 in the afternoon, but it felt like an eternity. It couldn't have been more than two or three hours, but it felt like a very long time that we were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you returned to the stadium, could you explain to the Trial Chamber what transpired.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: When I returned to the stadium? Before that, I was in their military hospital, in the medical centre, for about 25 days. And then when I arrived at the stadium, I was placed in a room and they call it the shock room, where I found those who had been beaten. And they put us who had arrived from the military hospital there. Again, it was terrible. Names would be called out. During the day, people would be taken to work on the front lines. Some 200 or so of us would stay in the camp and the remaining 100 or so would be taken to the front lines to work there. They would bring them back. They would be replaced by other people, all according to some list that I don't know who compiled. And then in the evening, again terror; individual names would be called out. And when those people would respond, they would put plastic bags on their heads. They would take them out to the stadium. They would beat them up, and then they would return them to the shock room, just like animals. They would just shove them into the room, all black and blue from beating.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And hence my reason that I asked you the question before, but I think you probably didn't understand. And the question I'll ask again is: Before you were taken to the stadium, you indicated to us a while ago that you went to the stadium from an outpatients clinic, from a hospital. Did you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: That is correct. I'll try to explain that very briefly. We were beaten up there at the cemetery, and it was the matter of life and death. My cousin, Mario, died on the way to our destination. As soon as they put him in the van, he died. I was left behind in the grammar school. I was thrown on the floor of the sports hall. There was nobody there. I wailed. I screamed. I asked for help. I even asked them to kill me. Their policeman, Bevrnja, came. I will never forget him. I believe he was the commander of the police. I asked him to help me. And he asked me, "What happened to you? Did you slip? Did you fall?" He was taunting me. And after a while, his nurse came. They turned me around, and she said that I had to be taken urgently to their military hospital in the military centre -- in the medical centre of Bugojno. Two police officers came. I believe that they were from Prusac. They were really correct and fair to me. They treated me with respect. They took me to the military hospital. Dr. Karadza took charge of me and examined me and it was upon his insistence that I stayed in the hospital and that's how I managed to survive. He locked me up in a special room. He gave me a guard who guarded me. Two days later he put me in a different room where other HVO soldiers were brought from those, so to say, reception centres, from the furniture salon and so forth. Four or five people came from the furniture salon. They were all beaten, just like me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And your cousin Mario Zrno, could you tell us what eventually happened to him.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: He died and they took him away. That's what they told me. That's what I could understand. They said that they were taking him to the grammar school, but it turned out that they buried him in the cemetery in Crnice, where quite a lot of them were buried, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. So now we're going to go forward to where you took us to a while ago. And I'd like you to describe for the Trial Chamber the conditions at the Iskra Stadium for us, please.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: As for the conditions at the stadium, again this was terrible. The bare stands made of concrete; underneath the stands, there was a PVC foil. We had a blanket each. It was just terrible. I have to say that sometime in the course of September we all got ill. We had lice. They had to cut our hair and shave us. It was terrible. And the most terrible thing of all was the accommodation, in a huge room which was about 80 square metres big, and there were 150 of us there. And when we returned from the place where we worked, they would put us in that room. And there was a barbed wire. There was just one bathroom in the whole of this stadium, and there were a total of 200 or so of us who were there most of the time. So can you imagine? No water, no electricity. As for the food, there was just one big pot with some boiled vegetables and maybe ten loaves of bread, so basically we fought for the food, and those who managed to eat something would develop diarrhoea immediately. Owing to the Croatian civilians who remained in Bugojno, still we managed to survive because they used all the possible channels to deliver some food, some bread to us. They helped us in any way they possibly could.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, you indicated to us that they took you out for work; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: For how long did you stay away from the stadium doing work?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I was there for 14 or 15 days, but I believe that it was 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: On your return to the stadium, could you describe for the Trial Chamber the conditions that existed.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Up to the end of November, it was really difficult. And during the first month, it was very difficult. This gradually subsided. However, we were always scared, always afraid that we would be taken away and beaten. People were being taken away every day for interrogation to the BH Bank. Some people never returned. The whereabouts of some 20 or so people are not known to the very day. Towards the end of the year, we were hoping that there would be an exchange around Christmas. There were stories about a possible exchange, but nothing came out of it. After new year, it became somewhat easier. We were not taken for work; we were not beaten. Their guards would come to talk to us. We had a lot more freedom. We were even brought some books to read, a chess board, playing cards. We would sometimes even be allowed to go outside and light a cigarette and go for a short walk. And this lasted for some three months, up to the 19th of March, when we were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us -- you indicated to us that people were taken out for beatings. Could you tell us by whom these people were taken out.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: The guards would call out names, and then they would put plastic bags on the heads of the people that they called out, and then they would take them to the stadium. Now, who did the actual beating, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, these guards, who were they?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: The Muslim army, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber how they were dressed.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: They wore the uniforms of the BiH army, camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And as time passed, did the numbers increase or decrease? Did the numbers of detainees increase or did they decrease?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: It increased, but not a lot. Not by a great number. In October or November, they brought two lads from Imotski who were put in a separate room. I believe that they had been captured in Gornji Vakuf. And they also brought a guy called Dedo from Prozor. One or two detainees were released earlier with the help of the Imam of Zagreb, Sefko Omerbasic, and some other priests. There were some secret links or connections, that these people managed to be released after five or six months.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Along with the guards that you told us that were Muslims, were there any other people from -- who may have been from other units in the compound?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I could not tell the difference between their units. They all wore identical uniforms. There were some individuals whom I remember who wore a Mujahedin uniform, and he had a sabre. He wanted to come towards the detainees and the guards prevented him from doing that. I was surprised. I don't know whether he was a Mujahedin or not, but he had a different uniform on. There was intimidation and terror all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And with the coming of the new year, did the situation change in the stadium?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: In 1994, it was somewhat easier and the situation changed as of new year. They treated us with a bit more respect. They would allow us to go out, to stretch our legs. We could also use the makeshift toilets that were outside the compound of the stadium. So it was a lot more bearable.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were eventually released?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: On the 19th of March, the exchange took place. They put us on lorries like cattle and they took us to Mostar, which was 150 kilometres away on a macadam road, and that's where they brought us and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did you eventually reconnect with your wife and family?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes. My wife and children were refugees in Tomislavgrad. I found them there. I spent a month or a month and a half there, and it was very fortunate that a friend of mine contacted me from Zagreb and offered me a job, which I accepted without any hesitation. So I thank God and this friend of mine that I am here today. I have built a house. In the meantime, I sold my house in Bugojno -- that is, I gave it away. I managed to give my children a roof over their head, and I am trying to make do with what I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Where do you reside presently?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: In Ceseta [phoen], which is a suburb of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Zrno, do you have any intentions of returning to Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Never. Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: State for the Trial Chamber how you felt upon your release from Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: There -- there are no words to describe that. I was almost unconscious. I was almost incapable of grasping the fact that I was with my wife, my children. They had beaten my spirit out of me. I was half-dead. I was -- all the time I was scared that I would never survive. I always feared for my life. There was even an operation that I didn't mention. When I was kept in the hospital, the rest were taken away, and as they were travelling -- the 150 men were travelled to Rabe, and the goal was for them to be killed there - that's what I heard - but the army from Prusac, the Muslim army from Prusac did not allow that and that -- these people were then returned to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Today, presently, how do you feel now?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to have to go through all this again; however, having said that, I also feel much more at ease. I have already started shaking. I don't know what to tell you. Let God be their judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this concludes the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mrs. Benjamin. The Defence counsel may begin their cross-examination. We have about half an hour before our first break.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Zrno. My name is Edina Residovic, and I represent General Hadzihasanovic. I'm really very sorry that during the war you suffered all those things that you testified about; however, in the interest of justice, I have to ask you some questions, and I would kindly ask you to answer those questions. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To the questions put to you by my learned friend, you said that during the war in 1993 you were a member of the HVO. Is it true that you became a member of the HVO on the 14th of August, 1992 and that you remained a member of the HVO until the moment you were captured? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that you became a guard in the military hospital in Bugojno and that you were captured in that position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to know whether you acted as a guard in this military hospital as a member of the police of the HVO or were you a guard -- a brigade guard?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I was a brigade guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that the relationship between the Croat and Muslim population in Bugojno deteriorated in the spring of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The incidents that started occurring at the time were mostly resolved by peaceful means; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, is it also correct that not far from Bugojno, in Gornji Vakuf, there was an armed conflict going on between the BiH army and the HVO and in April there were also conflicts in the Lasva Valley and this aggravated the situation between the Muslims and Croats in Bugojno? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have also mentioned an incident which took place around the 18th of July, when you heard from your colleagues that at the checkpoint in Vrbanja, not far from Bugojno, there had been an incident and that two members of the HVO - or better say the anti-terrorist detachment - were killed. Their names we Mico Vucak and Miroslav Telenta. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In accordance with previous attempts to resolve all incidents in a peaceful manner, a mixed commission of the BH MUP and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna MUP was formed; however, the commission was attacked, two MUP members were killed, and then the village of Vrbanja was also attacked; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I don't know about that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that a number -- a large number of civilians were killed in Vrbanja and 54 civilians were killed and the conflict then spread to the entire town?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that fighting went on for a number of days and throughout that period of time you were in the Kalin Hotel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from your brigade, the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade, in the spring of 1993 a home guard battalion was formed in Bugojno; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of the fighting, some members of the home guard battalion from the village of Gaj came to the hotel -- to Hotel Kalin. They came together with some civilians from that village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The HVO military police was located in the Kalin Hotel, and they resisted at all times and participated in the fighting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of the fighting, the wounded and the sick were evacuated from the hospital, but the military police continued to defend the Hotel Kalin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the shooting was terrible. Would it be correct to say that from the territory of Gorica, that is to say, from Tito's -- the territory of Tito's villa, the artillery also shelled the town and Hotel Kalin and one shell hit the hotel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I apologise, but I am not aware of that artillery shell hitting the hotel, but there was shooting from all side. I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you surrendered on Saturday, so about five or six days of fighting. And the soldiers you surrendered to in the Hotel Kalin treated you correctly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So far - and this is what you said yourself - you have given statements on a number of occasions about what you experienced. Did you give statements to the Prosecution of the Tribunal on the 29th of July and the 21st of September, 2000?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before that, like many others who have been imprisoned in prisons in Bugojno, you had also given a statement to Stjepan Vukadin, a lawyer from Bugojno; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We've been asked to slow down a bit, because it's necessary to wait for my question to be interpreted, and then you can answer. Thank you. As you have already said -- you spoke about events that you witnessed or experienced, but certain things - for example, which BH army units were involved or what the structure of the army was - these are things you are not personally familiar with; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also weren't familiar with the structure or the chain of command, the hierarchy in the police in Bugojno; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, at that time many people in Bugojno wore camouflage uniforms and as a result it was difficult to tell who belonged to an army unit or to the reserve MUP force; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. However, there was a difference between the uniforms of the Croatian army and the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I didn't even mention the HVO. You have already spoken about this, explained this to us. You were taken to the Gimnazija and you spent three or four days in the basement, which you've described when answering questions put to you by my learned colleague; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were then taken to the sports hall. And would it be correct to say that while you were there, while you were in the Gimnazija, you were visited by Sister Pavka and by European monitors?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the name of Bevrnja. And have I understood you correctly? You said that he was the chief of the guards in the Gimnazija.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: No, you misunderstood me. He was the chief of the police, of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I said that he was one of the persons in charge of the reserve police force, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I don't care what he was. He wasn't a man.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't know who decided that the Gimnazija should be used to detain prisoners there, nor did you know at the time who was in charge of the facility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: There's no reason for you not to agree with me if I say that the Gimnazija was under the control of the civilian police until October 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't agree with you. Your military police were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I haven't understood you correctly. I didn't have a military police force.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: The military police of the BH army was in the Gimnazija, and it was in the Koprivica building too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you know something about the army.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the town, so I should know something about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So your answer to my previous question was perhaps not quite precise. Thank you for your additional clarification. You don't know who decided that the Iskra Stadium should be transformed into a temporary prison for prisoners of war. Likewise, you didn't know who was in charge of it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No one physically maltreated you in the Gimnazija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And when you were at the Iskra Stadium, no one took you out and physically maltreated you either; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that on the 30th of July you reported for work as a volunteer in town. Is it correct that at the time Mladen Barnjak, Berislav Dzalto [as interpreted], Perica Sistov, Ivica Bartulovic, Mladen Brkic were with you? And when you were involved in this work and as you passed through Bugojno, you also saw Mario Zrno, Milos Zeljko, Dragan Keskic and others who were prisoners at the time. These were persons you knew and saw there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While you were digging the graves, there was an armed guard accompanying you, and he treated you fairly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, someone who fled from us five minutes after he had taken us there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After 10 or 15 people from Vrbanja came and started to beat you, you soon lost consciousness, as you were weak, so you were in fact not really aware of what actually happened there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Well, I know quite a few things and there are quite a few things that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, after you were taken back to the Gimnazija, as you said, after a certain period of time had elapsed, you were taken to the hospital and were provided with medical treatment there. You remained there until the 25th of August there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Later you found out that your relative Mario Zrno died in Perica Sistov's lap; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: No, it wasn't in the same lorry. We were thrown into the same lorry together, and that's where I found out about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you managed to survive thanks to the fact that some civilians in the town managed to provide you with food in various ways, and those who received the food were able to share it with others. This is how they helped everyone survive those very difficult times. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, Sister Pavka would also visit you and she would bring some essential items with her and sometimes food as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Sometimes, but that occurred very infrequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: She was also accompanied by a doctor, who provided you -- or who provided the prisoners with certain medicine if they needed such medicine; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes. They would provide them with Undol [phoen], which are pills, painkillers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you heard that on one occasion they were supposed to take a certain number of prisoners somewhere; however, you in fact don't have any direct, firsthand information about this.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: No, I can't talk about things that I have no direct information of.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that a group of Croatian intellectuals asked that you not be transferred to the KP Dom in Zenica? They wanted you to remain in Bugojno because they were afraid that something might happen to you on the way.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You are aware of the fact that a significant number of Croats returned to Bugojno and they are now living in that town without any particular problems; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I haven't been to Bugojno myself, and I don't want to go there either. As far as I am aware, very few Croats have returned there and they aren't living very well. It's very difficult for them to find jobs, so I don't know what kind of a life that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zrno.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now give the floor to the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Judges have Some questions for the witness, but first of all, I would like to ask Ms. Benjamin whether she has any further questions now that the Defence has concluded their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. To avoid spoiling the rhythm, I think it would be best to have the break now, and we will resume at about five to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume. The Judges have a few questions for you based on the answers you provided to both parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will go back to the time at which you became an HVO member. When you became an HVO member, did you have the status of a member of the military then or were civilian Croats concerned, they were asked to have a uniform and weapon in order to defend the town and to guard the hospital? In your opinion, what was your status? Were you still a civilian or had you actually become a real member of the military?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I became a real HVO soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And did you have a rank? Were you a member of a unit with a commander? What was the situation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Well, I was attached to the command of the Eugen Kvaternik Unit. I was a soldier whose duty was to work as a guard of the military hospital. I was an ordinary soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to guard the hospital, what sort of a weapon did you have? Did you have a rifle? Did you have a machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I had a Kalashnikov. Our task was to be performed without the use of weapons. We were to take care of the people entering the hospital and they weren't supposed to enter the building with weapons. We would put these weapons away in cupboards, et cetera, and then we would return them when they left. We helped take charge of the wounded when they arrived. Rifles weren't used, and that wasn't our task. It wasn't actually necessary, because the hospital was a joint hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You said that you surrendered and that you laid down your weapon. When you surrendered, who did you surrender to? Do you remember who you surrendered to exactly?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: There were at least 30 to 40 soldiers there. I don't remember their faces at all. I don't even think that these people were people from Bugojno, because if any of them were from Bugojno, I would have recognised them. After having lived for 15 years in Bugojno, I can recognise certain faces. These troops were from other towns in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There were hardly any soldiers who were from Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 30 or 40 soldiers you mentioned, you said in response to a question put to you a while ago that they had green uniforms and they had armbands. Did you see any insignia on their uniforms indicating the unit to which they belonged?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: The only insignia they had -- well, all they had were these lilies representing the BH army. That's what their name was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have understood you correctly, if I am following you, you surrendered to soldiers who were members of the BH army because they had a lily symbol on their uniforms. That is what you are saying. They were therefore soldiers from the BH army.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: That's what they called themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you able to speak to these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you went to the detention facility -- because we know, as you said a minute ago, that you were detained. You said that it was a very bad experience -- the people who guarded you, were they the same soldiers who had arrested you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The men guarding you, did they also have uniforms with insignia on them or not?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, they did have uniforms with insignia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The insignia they had on their uniforms, were these insignia of the same kind as those that you saw on the 30 or 40 soldiers who had arrested you? Did they have the same kind of insignia on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the men guarding you, were they people from Bosnia and Herzegovina or were they inhabitants who perhaps didn't live in Bugojno, perhaps they lived in some other town? Were they people from Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: In the Iskra Stadium, the people were from Bosnia and Herzegovina and they were mostly people from Bugojno, people whom I knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but the soldiers who guarded you, were they from the region? Were they your compatriots? Were they from Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes. As I have already said, yes, the people at the stadium who guarded us were people from Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As you were a member of the military, you were guarded by members of the military. Were you questioned and was the questioning conducted in accordance with the Geneva Conventions concerning prisoners of war? Did they ask you for your name and the unit that you belonged to? Were you questioned?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, we were questioned by their superiors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what were you asked when you were questioned? What sort of information were you asked to provide?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Naturally, they asked us which unit we belonged to. They asked us whether we had been in action. They wanted to know what sort of things we had been involved in and where we had been during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A minute ago, in response to the Defence counsel -- a Defence counsel question you said that you personally hadn't been beaten or tortured. You were speaking about yourself.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I think you have misunderstood something. I was beaten. I was hit at the Vrbanja cemetery while we were digging graves there, and as a result I had to spend 25 days in the hospital. I barely remained alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was going to mention this incident at the cemetery, but my question concerned the detention facility -- the detention facilities; that is to say, it concerned the Gimnazija and the stadium. I'll now address the issue of the cemetery. You said that you went to the cemetery to work. Could you tell us what this work consisted of.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: As far as I myself am -- are concerned and my four colleagues, we dug graves so that they could bury their dead. It was by the River Vrbas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was to bury the dead. Dead members of the HVO or dead members of the BH army? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I think that these people were Muslim civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they were Muslim civilians. Why were you beaten, since you had been taken there to dig graves? Could you tell us the reason for which you were beaten.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: If I only knew I wouldn't be so embittered. Unfortunately, these people knew me well. They all knew who I was, what I did, and they knew that I didn't make a distinction between Croats, Serbs, and Muslims. I couldn't work. I was exhausted. I couldn't stand on my two feet. I had suffered and they beat me. Why? You have to ask them. I don't know. I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those who beat you, did they wear uniforms or did they wear camouflage uniforms? And did they bear the insignia of the army?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: They wore the BiH army uniforms. Among them, there were also the military police belonging to the BiH army. You could recognise them by the white belts that they had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you have explained to us that in the cemetery you were beaten. There were two groups of soldiers: There were the BiH army soldiers and there were also some other soldiers who were military police, who wore the typical white belts. What did the military police do, according to you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Well, they came to kill us. There were some blood ties involved. The Velagic family were there who had committed the crime [as interpreted], and they were aware that none of us did anything wrong. I didn't do anything wrong and Mario didn't do anything wrong. And they knew that that was the case with everybody else who was in the cemetery. Because in Bugojno everything is known; they knew who did what and they knew that we didn't have anything to do with the killings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have just told us that the military police who were there and who beat you actually came to retaliate because of what had happened to others and that you were the one that they suspected that had to do with the crimes that had taken place. Is that what you told me?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: They could not suspect that. They knew where I was and what I did. Even this military policeman, Safet Velagic, was in the military hospital with me three days before the conflict and we had a long conversation about all sorts of things. So he knew who I was, where I was, and what I did. They did not suspect me. They didn't want to take their vengeance on me. They were just carried away by the victory. They were grieving for the members of their family, which is understandable. However, what I can't understand is that somebody could beat another human being who had been beaten already, who had been weakened, exhausted. And I can't forgive them that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have told us that the military policeman whom you knew, whose name was Safet Velagic --

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this Safet Velagic was present in the cemetery and he was present at the moment when you were beaten there. Is that what you have told us?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the cemetery where you were with others performing some work, you told us that you were exhausted. How many of you -- actually, how many military policemen and soldiers were there at the time? How many troops were there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I believe that there were five or six men there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Among those five or six, did you see somebody who acted as a leader or were they all the same? Was there anybody with a certain authority who issued commands or orders to those who guarded you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: There was nobody. Muhko Velagic was in charge and he was the one who was involved in the incident. He was the one who beat me and Mario the most, and it was under his orders that all of those things happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are telling us that Muhko Velagic was the person who seemed to have been in charge.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Muhko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it Muhko or Vuko?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: M-u-h-k-o, Muhko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were injured and you were then taken to the hospital. That's what you told us.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the hospital, did you tell either the doctor or somebody else what had happened? Did you tell them that you had been injured and how it had happened? Did you tell that to those who looked after you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes. I explained everything to Dr. Karadza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You explained everything to Dr. Karadza. And Dr. Karadza, was he a military doctor or was he a civilian?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Dr. Karadza was a member of the HVO, an HVO doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was an HVO doctor. And Dr. Karadza, what did he tell you after that, after you had told him what had happened? What did he tell you? Is -- did he tell you that he is going to inform somebody else, some other authorities? What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Dr. Karadza examined me and he separated me from the others on his own initiative. The police officers were reluctant to leave me there because then they had their orders to return me to the Gimnazija. But Dr. Karadza negotiated them [as interpreted] and managed to keep me in the hospital. I don't think anybody dared tell him anything. And I didn't have any visitors. Nobody dared visit me. My friends didn't visit me. I don't know whether Dr. Karadza managed to inform anybody or not, but I don't think he dared talk about anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that the police officers, the military police departed, they left the hospital, and they went to the school. They left you in the hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A little while ago in replying to a question you were talking about your relative, Mario, and you explained that you were in the lorry together with him, in the van. Can you please be more specific about what you told us a little while ago.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: The two of us had been beaten at the same time. When I fainted, he would be beaten; and the other way around. After all the beatings, we were thrown together into a lorry. I was really in a bad shape. Mario was even in a worse shape. Perica Sistov took him in his lap. He tried to help him. Four or five minutes later on the way back to the reception camp Mario succumbed to his wounds. He died.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are telling us that as a result of the beatings you and your relative were in a bad shape. You were thrown into that vehicle, the van, and that in that van your relative died and you witnessed the death of your relative in this van. You saw that.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you saw him. You saw that he wasn't moving, that he was dead.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: My other colleagues who were in the van, Perica Sistov and others, established the fact that he was dead and they told me that he was dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the van -- I'm trying to follow what you're telling us. When you were taken to the hospital, what happened to the body of your relative who -- which was in the van at the time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I've already explained. They did not bring the van to the hospital. The van stayed by the grammar school and my relative was taken to the medical centre in the convent. He belonged to the 1st Battalion. There were several reception centres or reception camps. There were several locations where people were received. I don't know how many there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In responding your question -- to a question, you said that you were liberated after having spent several months in detention. When you were liberated, were you given a piece of paper, a document? What did they tell you on the day when you were made a free man again? What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: We did not receive any papers. The only thing that happened while we were in the camp was that the Red Cross came and made a list of our names and they gave us a number each. We didn't receive any paper after that. We were only told to report to the hospital and be examined there. And at that moment, we only wanted to feel free again and to be joined with our families, so I don't think that any of us actually went to the hospital to be examined. That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you are telling us happened ten years ago, but it seems that you're still suffering some psychological consequences of what happened to you. Are you under any medical care? Do you still suffer any consequences? Do you still have some problems as a result of what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I did seek medical help for five or six years. I was doing it in vain. Finally I was told that I was a hypochondriac, so I stopped seeking medical help. I am working. I'm trying to live with my family, and we'll see how it goes. I'm not under any medical care at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the other Judges if they have any questions to put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Just two or three follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please. Microphone for Judge Swart, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Just two or three follow-up questions. You told us about the fact that you were beaten and that your nephew was also beaten, and you told us also that you were then treated in the hospital for 25 days, if I understand well. What were your wounds? What were ...?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I was black and blue from my loins up to my head. I had problems with my kidneys, with urination. I am still suffering some problems with my spine, because I had a haematoma on my back and I still feel the consequences, and I don't even want to go into the psychological problems that I still have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Have you also broken some ribs or arms or bones or ...?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: No, I didn't suffer any fractures, no, luckily enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And your family member, Mario, has he fractures?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I don't know. I wouldn't be able to tell you. He was exhumed only five or six years after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... by fists or by feet or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: The rifle butt, boots, stones, police battalions, everything, everything. They treated him like an animal. They were animals. The way they treated him was totally inhumane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: If I understood you well, you had been volunteering to work outside the place where you were held, detained.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Is this also true for your work at the graveyard, the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: If you volunteered to do these things and you are -- and you are beaten, then I suppose you don't want to do this again.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I would never have volunteered if I had known, but I didn't know it. I volunteered because Mladen Barnjak, a colleague of mine who often volunteered and went with these groups, told me that they were sent to the Croatian houses to collect food and that this was an opportunity for them to change clothes and to have some food, and that's what I thought would happen if I volunteer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But you did work there for 15 days, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: I'm afraid that's not what happened. The cemetery is one thing and the 15 days that I spent working was on the front line, where I was digging trenches, and that is the 15-day period that I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And how many days did you work at the cemetery, then?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: It was two, three, or four hours. Hours, not days. However, it seemed like an eternity to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I see. And this was also on the basis of voluntary work?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence counsel, do you have any questions that arise from the Judges' questions? You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do have a few questions, but I don't know whether before that my learned friend is going to be given the opportunity to put questions to the witness, so who is going to be first? I am -- since this is a Prosecution witness ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Since this is a Prosecution question, the Prosecution will be given the floor after you, so you will have the floor first; the Prosecution will follow; and then if there are any additional questions, we'll see what -- how we go about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you told me a little while ago that Dragan Keskic, Perica Sistov, your cousin Mario, Zeljko Milos and others worked in the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your cousin Mario died, but the other persons also witnessed what had happened there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: They also would not have any reason to represent the situation in any other way than it really happened.

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These persons were also interviewed by the lawyer Vukadin about the things that they lived there; are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to put to you that Perica Sistov in his statement that he gave to the lawyer mentioned that while you worked you were guarded by six guards -- actually, while the six of you worked, there were two guards with you and that these two did not provoke you, did not ill-treat you in any way, they gave you water and cigarettes, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If Perica Sistov would also say that at the time when the other 14 prisoners came, amongst whom Mario Zrno, that at that time or a bit later some other men, Muslim men came, amongst whom Zilhad Hodzic from Vrbanja, whose father worked in the gas station, and also Mujo Pelagic [phoen] who was the owner of a restaurant. That's when the ill-treatment started, and the only person who did not ill-treat you was Zilhad Hodzic. He didn't do that because we worked together and he took a distance from the group and only observed what was going on. "I can't confirm who were the persons beating Mario, because -- Zrno -- because I didn't know these people or I knew them only superficially. I believe that those people who lived with them in Vrbanja could confirm that because they knew them." And if I told you that Perica Sistov said all that, would that be the correct description of what happened?

utterances.speaker: VINKO ZRNO
utterances.text: Yes, this is a correct description, because they turned our backs to the guards. They were ordered not to look in their faces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zrno, if Dragan Keskic described the same event in the following way: "Members of the Muslim army and civilians who had died during the conflicts and whose bodies had to be buried, obviously this was the area of conflict and it was not easy to tell who was a soldier, who was a civilian, and who was shooting and who was not. Our men were sent there. Mario Zrno was one of them.
